Source. The long-option helper copies the attacker-controlled payload after `--` into a mutable config buffer. For the staged witness that payload is tabs, the token `enum`, another tab, and four `0xff` bytes.

Because the copied payload contains no `=` and no literal space character, this helper takes its fallback path and appends `" 1"`. The resulting config text is `\t...\tenum\t\xff\xff\xff\xff 1`, which creates the later standalone numeric token `1`.
The synthetic config line from step 2 is duplicated into the config memory list, preserving it for deferred processing during `init_snmp()`.

When `read_configs()` replays remembered config lines, it feeds the stored attacker-controlled line back into the config parser. This is the order edge that reconnects the deferred config text to the vulnerable parser path.

The config parser tokenizes the remembered line on spaces, tabs, and `=`. This skips the leading tabs and extracts `enum` as the directive token, selecting the enum configuration path for the same attacker-controlled line.

Handler lookup finds the config handler registered as `register_const_config_handler(type, "enum", se_read_conf, NULL, NULL)`, so `run_config_handler()` invokes `se_read_conf()` with `token == "enum"` and the remaining argument string `\xff\xff\xff\xff 1`.

Inside `se_read_conf()`, the first remaining token is copied into `e_name` as the four-byte string `\xff\xff\xff\xff`. That string does not match `major:minor`, so execution falls through to the named-enumeration branch.

The next token in the named-enumeration branch is copied into the fixed stack buffer `e_enum`. Because step 2 appended `" 1"`, this copy materializes the short NUL-terminated string `"1"` in `e_enum`.

This check only requires `%d` to assign successfully. For `e_enum == "1"`, `sscanf` stores `value == 1` and returns 1 even though no colon follows, so the parser continues on a token that has a numeric prefix but no separator.

Root cause step. `cp2` starts at `e_enum`, but this loop checks only for `':'` and not for the terminating NUL. With `e_enum == "1"`, it reads the `'1'`, then the NUL, then keeps advancing through the rest of the stack buffer looking for a colon that does not exist.

Root cause. The colon-scan loop checks only for `':'` and does not stop when `cp2` reaches the terminating NUL of `e_enum`, so a token like `"1"` makes the scan walk off the fixed stack buffer.
